headline: DOL Rule to Raise H-1B Wages Found Likely Illegal, Would Disqualify 80% of Current Offers
subheadline: A Cato Institute analysis finds the Department of Labor's proposed prevailing wage hike — averaging $26,000 per worker — exceeds statutory authority and lacks empirical basis, threatening hundreds of thousands of visa holders already in the U.S.
body:
• The Cato Institute finds DOL's proposed rule to nearly double H-1B entry-level wage thresholds is legally questionable, citing no empirical basis and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act.
  • Over 80% of current H-1B wage offers — including the highest-skilled workers — would be disqualified under the new percentile thresholds, with average prevailing wages rising roughly $26,000 annually.
  • The rule arrives amid a broader federal crackdown: DHS ended duration-of-status protections on July 17, a $100,000 H-1B fee is under consideration, and the DOL Inspector General is pursuing fraud investigations.
  • Indian nationals, who receive approximately 70% of all H-1B approvals, face disproportionate impact — particularly workers already in the U.S. for years who could be priced out of their own jobs.

A proposed Department of Labor rule that would sharply increase mandatory minimum wages for H-1B visa holders is likely illegal and rests on no identified market failure, according to an analysis published by the Cato Institute. The finding adds a legal dimension to the most aggressive federal assault on the H-1B program in decades.

David Bier, associate director of immigration studies at Cato, concluded the rule "provides no empirical basis for raising the prevailing wage" and would force out hundreds of thousands of workers who have lived in the United States for years. The analysis argues it exceeds DOL's statutory authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act.

What DOL Wants to Change

Under the proposed rule (RIN 1205-AC30), DOL would raise prevailing wage floors across all four federally mandated skill levels. Level 1 wages for entry-level workers would jump from the 17th to the 34th percentile of the occupational wage distribution. Level 2 moves from the 34th to 52nd percentile, Level 3 from 50th to 70th, and Level 4 — for "fully competent" workers — from the 67th to the 88th percentile.

The average H-1B prevailing wage would rise approximately $26,000 annually. According to Cato's modeling, more than 80% of current H-1B job offers would fail the new thresholds — including the vast majority at the highest skill level. For software developers, the most common H-1B occupation, the disqualification rate is similarly severe.

The Legal Case Against It

"DOL never even offers a theoretical basis for an increase in the prevailing wage. The market sets wages based on marginal productivity."

— David Bier, Cato Institute

The legal challenge rests on several pillars. DOL's own data show H-1B workers earn an average premium of $10,191 above current prevailing wages — evidence that competitive market forces are already functioning. Cato found entry-level wages for H-1B-eligible workers sit at about the 19th percentile, close to the current 17th-percentile threshold and well below the proposed 34th.

Cato also points to congressional intent. When Congress mandated four wage levels in 2004, it ratified the existing structure. Asserting 22 years later that the same framework requires wages that ban most job offers contradicts that legislative history. DOL's alternative "experience benchmarking" methodology fares no better — it would also exclude over 80% of offers.

Impact on Indian Workers

Indian nationals received roughly 70% of all approved H-1B petitions in recent years. The wage floors would hit Indian IT services firms — Infosys, Cognizant, Tata Consultancy Services — particularly hard, as they employ large numbers of Level 1 and Level 2 workers.

The pain extends beyond outsourcing firms. Indian-born engineers at Microsoft, Amazon, and Google who have built lives in the U.S. over a decade could find their compensation suddenly below the new prevailing wage, making visa renewals impossible. For workers in India's green card backlog — which stretches decades — the rule could end their time in the country before permanent residency ever arrives.

A Broader Crackdown

The wage rule does not exist in isolation. On July 17, DHS ended "duration of status" — the policy that let international students remain in the U.S. for the length of their program. A four-year cap now applies, with extensions requiring formal USCIS approval. Brookings warned the change could cost the U.S. economy $72–145 billion annually over ten years.

The administration has also proposed a $100,000 H-1B fee, and DOL Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito has launched fraud investigations with dozens of subpoenas. Microsoft's approval of 2,273 H-1B workers in the same period it cut 4,800 jobs — including 1,600 from Xbox — further inflamed the political debate. There are currently 730,000 H-1B holders in the United States.

What Happens Next

The proposed rule remains in its public comment period. Given Cato's legal analysis and the likelihood of industry litigation, the proposal faces a contested path. Courts have previously struck down similar DOL wage rules for overstepping statutory bounds.

For roughly half a million Indian-born H-1B workers and their families, the calculus is grimly familiar: higher fees, tighter enforcement, shorter stays, and now wage floors that could price them out of jobs they already hold.
